items.body:
MAINZ. **In den Pausen sollen Kinder und Jugendliche spielen oder mehr miteinander sprechen, statt Nachrichten zu schreiben – meint die rheinland-pfälzische Bildungsministerin. Sie hat dafür neue Regeln für den Gebrauch von Handys in Schulen erlassen. Recht strenge: Bis einschließlich 10. Klasse gilt bald für Schülerinnen und Schüler ein Verbot privater Nutzung von Smartphones. Die Schülervertretung zeigt sich wenig begeistert.**

Und – weg. (Symbolfoto) Foto: Shutterstock

Handys, iPads, Smartwatches und Smartbrillen sind für Schülerinnen und Schüler bis Ende der 10. Klasse ab dem zweiten Halbjahr an den Schulen in Rheinland-Pfalz für die private Nutzung tabu. Bei der Regelung gehe es um internetfähige digitale Endgeräte, sagte Bildungsministerin Ute Eiling-Hütig (CDU) in Mainz.

Ausnahmen gebe es, wenn die Smartphones und iPads für Lehr- und Lernzwecke verwendet werden, aus gesundheitlichen Gründen sowie etwa auf Klassenfahrten, wenn die Kinder und Jugendlichen dringend bei ihren Eltern anrufen möchten. Das entschieden dann die betreuenden Lehrkräfte, erklärte Eiling-Hütig.

## Mittagspause regeln die Schulen

In die Entscheidung der Schulen falle auch die private Nutzung der internetfähigen digitalen Endgeräte in der Mittagspause beim Ganztag. Ansonsten gelte auch für den schulischen Nachmittag das private Handy-Verbot, sagte die Bildungsministerin.

Ob die Schülerinnen und Schüler ihre Geräte abgeben und etwa in einen Spind packen müssen oder ausgeschaltet in der Tasche haben, liege dann im Ermessen der Schulen. Da mache das Bildungsministerium keine Vorgaben, sagte die CDU-Politikerin.

## Berufliche Schulen signalisieren auch Interesse

Das Vorhaben gelte auch für die Förderschulen in Rheinland-Pfalz. Die beruflichen Schulen seien nicht dabei. Es gebe aber bereits positive Rückmeldungen mit Interesse für eine Einführung der Handy-Regeln. Bei den Oberstufen werde es genauso gehandhabt wie mit der Mittagspause, erklärte Eiling-Hütig: Es liege in der Entscheidung der Schulen.

Die finale detaillierte Umsetzung der neuen Regeln werde nach Abschluss der Verbändeanhörung festgelegt. Innerhalb der Koalition mit der SPD seien die Beschlüsse kein großes Streitthema gewesen, versicherte die Christdemokratin.

## Landesschülervertretung weiter gegen Handy-Verbot

Die Landeschülerinnen und -schülervertretung (LSV) spricht sich nach Angaben der Ministerin weiterhin gegen die Maßnahmen aus. Ein pauschales Verbot greife zu kurz und ersetze keine pädagogischen Konzepte, argumentierte zuletzt die LSV. Die Kinder und Jugendlichen müssten lernen, verantwortungsvoll mit digitalen Medien umzugehen. Dafür brauche es eine stärkere Verankerung von Medienbildung und klare, gemeinsam entwickelte Regeln an Schulen.

Cybermobbing, problematische Inhalte oder exzessive Mediennutzung dürften nicht ignoriert werden. Doch pauschalen Handy-Verbote an Schulen sowie mögliche Social-Media-Verboten seien keine nachhaltige Lösung, mahnte die LSV. Sie beseitigten die Ursachen nicht, sondern würden die Probleme lediglich aus dem Blickfeld verschieben. Cybermobbing mache nicht vor der Schule halt und verschwinde nicht, wenn das Smartphone in die Tasche stecke.

## Vorbildfunktion für zu Hause

Der Landesregierung sei wichtig, dass sich die Kinder in den Pausen einfach in Präsenz miteinander beschäftigen. Es gehe um das Vertiefen der sozialen Kompetenzen. «Ich muss meiner Freundin vielleicht nicht eine WhatsApp schreiben, die zwei Meter weiter steht, sondern ich kann direkt mit ihr sprechen.»

Eiling-Hütig äußerte die Hoffnung, dass die neuen Handy-Regeln auch eine Vorbildfunktion für das Nutzungsverhalten der Kinder und Jugendlichen in der Freizeit hat. Eltern könnten dann argumentieren, dass das Weglegen der Smartphones und iPads zu Hause genauso wie in der Schule funktionieren könne.

## Plattformbetreiber im Fokus

Die Bildungsministerin sprach sich in der Diskussion über ein Social-Media-Verbot für bestimmte Altersgruppen dafür aus, die Plattformen mehr in die Verantwortung zu nehmen. Es könne nicht alleine die Aufgabe der Politik, der Eltern, Lehrkräfte sowie der Schülerinnen und Schüler sein, für Regelungen zu sorgen. Stattdessen müssten die Plattformbetreiber mehr in die Verpflichtung genommen werden. *News4teachers / mit Material der dpa*

> [Handy-Verbote reichen nicht: Leopoldina warnt vor Social-Media-Risiken – und fordert mehr Medienerziehung in Kitas und Schulen](https://www.news4teachers.de/2025/08/handy-verbote-allein-schuetzen-nicht-leopoldina-warnt-vor-social-media-risiken-und-fordert-mehr-medienkompetenz-in-kitas-und-schulen/)

## What I’m thankful for, literarily.

– Weird and in person celebrations of books.

– Listening to a poem while doing my little stretches. The Library of Congress and Poetry Archive collections, to be specific.

– And I’m thankful in advance to the programmer who builds me a little widget or website that streams a random poem from these archives.

– The new Marlon James . I’m late to the party, but damn.

– Finding something cool in a pile of books someone is giving away.

– The major book awards no longer being afraid of support for Palestine, and Paradiso 17 and Huna winning NBAs.

– A really good pen. I’ve had two instances recently where I had a small bookstore coupon that I spent on luxe pens. Highly recommend treating yourself to a fine writing instrument.

– Funny novels with funny first person narrators.

– The tide continuing to turn against AI. I’m thankful we may see AI’s high water mark very soon.

– Getting to interview Adam Peterson for the release of his story collection.

– Booksellers, who are in the middle of their most hectic season. I’m thankful for everyone who treats them reasonably this time of year.

– Peanuts, a Perfect Snack For Reading.

– Librarians, who are always in the middle of hectic season.

– Flaming Hydra , and especially Luke O’Neil’s recent New England Week which I’m revisiting as I pack up to go to Boston for the holiday.

– Connecting with a stranger over a book, especially that thing where someone points at your book from a distance, and you close it and hold up the cover, and they give you a thumbs up. Really good stuff.

– Small presses, and all the cool and weird things they’re taking a chance on.

– Marilynne Robinson . Her middle name is Summers, but she’s an autumn writer.

– My sweet seven month old showing preferences for books. And I also chew on the books that I like, so I’m thankful that he inherited that trait from me.

– Trying to explain Gene Wolfe ’s deal to someone for the first time.

– A small book you can read in an afternoon. Also having an afternoon free to read.

– Olga Ravn’s gift guide , which includes Ibuprofen and haunted dolls.

– Reading an author who is really going for it and trying something new. I appreciate someone taking a risk, regardless of the outcome. (Usually.)

– A friend asking for a book recommendation, and then actually reading your recommendation, and then telling you they liked your recommendation. No better feeling in the world.

### James Folta

James Folta is a staff writer at Lit Hub and the managing editor of Points in Case. He co-writes the weekly Newsletter of Humorous Writing. More at www.jamesfolta.com, or you can reach me at jfolta@lithub.com.

items.body:
Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten. Annette Leßmöllmann und Markus Weißkopf sprechen zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de über Erfolge, Herausforderungen und notwendigen Wandel.

Am 24. November 2016 ging Wissenschaftskommunikation.de online. In unserem [Schwerpunkt zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wo-steht-die-wisskomm/)blicken wir auf prägende Entwicklungen zurück *und fragen, wo die Wissenschaftskommunikation heute steht.*

**Mit welcher Idee und welchem persönlichen Anspruch seid Ihr 2016 an der Gründung von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de beteiligt gewesen?**

**Markus Weißkopf** ist Redakteur des Research.Table bei Table.Media. Er war Geschäftsführer von Wissenschaft im Dialog und hat dort unter anderem die Plattform Wissenschaftskommunikation.de aufgebaut. Foto: WiD

Markus Weißkopf: Kurz zuvor hatten Wissenschaft im Dialog und der Bundesverband Hochschulkommunikation gemeinsam die [Leitlinien zur guten Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/leitlinien-zur-guten-wissenschaftskommunikation-85129/) veröffentlicht. In dem Zuge hatte die Community viel über gemeinsame Werte, aber auch über die Professionalisierung der Wissenschaftskommunikation diskutiert. Wissenschaftskommunikation.de sollte unter anderem eine Plattform für diese Themen bieten.

Annette Leßmöllmann: Die Plattform sollte zeigen: Wissenschaftskommunikation bedeutet mehr als nur Pressemitteilungen und Hochglanzmagazine. Mir war es ein Anliegen, Forschung und Praxis zusammenzubringen und somit die [Vermittlung der Wissenschaftskommunikationsforschung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/kategorie/forschung/) voranzutreiben. Zum einen, um praxisrelevante Ergebnisse bekannt zu machen, zum anderen, um die theoretische Weiterentwicklung, die Interdisziplinarität und die Selbstreflexion des Forschungsfeldes zu zeigen. Gleichzeitig sollten Praxisfragen für die Forschung nachvollziehbar werden, um neue Forschung anzustoßen.

**Annette Leßmöllmann** (@annetteless.bsky.social) ist promovierte Linguistin und hat am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT)* den Lehrstuhl für Wissenschaftskommunikation mit dem Schwerpunkt Linguistik inne. Sie lehrt in den Bachelor- und Master-Studiengängen „Wissenschaft – Medien – Kommunikation“ (@WMKstudium).

**Welche Fragen oder Konfliktlinien aus der Gründungszeit beschäftigen die Community bis heute?**

Weißkopf: „Als Anlaufstelle Nr. 1 hat sich das Online-Lexikon Wikipedia im Internet längst etabliert. Die Wissenschaft sollte das Potenzial von Wikipedia für die Vermittlung fundierten Wissens ernsthaft prüfen.“ Das hat eine Pressesprecherin [im Rahmen des ersten Schwerpunkts „Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation“](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/blick-nach-vorn-wie-sieht-die-wissenschaftskommunikation-der-zukunft-aus-5-13517/) geschrieben. Natürlich ist das Prüfen wissenschaftsimmanent. Aber im Bereich der Kommunikation können wir es uns nicht erlauben, jahrelang zu prüfen. Die Wissenschaft hat nun ein Engagement bei oder für [Wikipedia](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/format/wikipedia/) so lange geprüft, bis es zu spät war. Nur einzelne Einrichtungen wie die Universität Innsbruck bilden hier Ausnahmen. Da würde ich mir manchmal mehr Mut zum Experimentieren wünschen!

Leßmöllmann: Was sich bereits vor zehn Jahren angekündigt hat: Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden. Dass sie in Interessenslagen und Machtstrukturen eingebettet ist und dass es als machtvoller kommunikativer Akt angesehen wird, wenn jemand „bestimmt“, was wahr oder falsch ist – das war damals eher ein Gedankenexperiment, ist heute aber deutlich als Konflikt zu spüren.

Es wird für die Wissenschaftskommunikation viel schwieriger, wenn es den Entscheider*innen reicht, dass sich etwas wahr anfühlt, auch wenn es nicht wahr ist. Dass etwa politische und gesellschaftliche Entscheidungen gegen den vorherrschenden wissenschaftlichen Konsens getroffen werden, ist angesichts der Klimakrise deutlich bedrohlicher und krisenhafter spürbar als noch vor zehn Jahren.

### „Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden.“

Annette Leßmöllmann

**Direkt mit dem ersten Schwerpunkt des Portals haben wir damals auf die** **[Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/zukunft-der-wissenschaftskommunikation/)** **geblickt. Welche damaligen Hoffnungen und Befürchtungen haben sich aus Eurer Sicht bewahrheitet und welche nicht?**

Leßmöllmann: Es hat sich die Hoffnung bewahrheitet, dass heute stärker darauf geachtet wird, Kommunikationsaktivitäten wissenschaftlich fundiert zu evaluieren. Zudem hat es funktioniert, dass sich die Community intensiver vernetzt und dass Forschung und Praxis enger zusammenarbeiten.

Es gab auch den Wunsch, dass Wissenschaftskommunikation stärker Teil der Gesellschaft und des täglichen Austauschs über die relevanten Themen der Zeit wird. In einem Aspekt hat sich der Wunsch bewahrheitet, allerdings anders als gedacht: Durch [generative Künstliche Intelligenz](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/themen/kuenstliche-intelligenz/) sind Wissen und Wissenschaft jetzt noch einfacher und dialogischer zu erreichen.

Gleichzeitig wurde die DIN-Norm der Kommunikation aufgeweicht: Es ist nicht mehr sicher, ob das Kommunizierte auch stimmt. Dies trägt zu einer Wissenskrise bei. Etwas dystopisch und pointiert formuliert: Gesagt und geglaubt wird, was gut klingt und auf die Interessen der eigenen Peer Group einzahlt. Das zeigt, dass wir in einer völlig anderen Welt als vor zehn Jahren leben. Die Rolle des Wissens, die demokratische Verankerung und die Wissenschaftsfreiheit stehen zur Debatte.

items.body:
# opt.in.ismus

Deadline: 05.01.2027

## opt.in.ismus

## Call for Particitpation für die re:publica 27 vom 10. bis 12. Mai 2027 in Berlin. Deadline: 5. Januar 2027

Es ist wieder soweit: Der Call for Participation zur re:publica 27 ist geöffnet!

Du hast eine Idee, ein Projekt, eine Recherche, ein Experiment oder eine künstlerische Intervention, die die digitale Gesellschaft voranbringt und im #rp27-Programm nicht fehlen darf? Dann bist du hier genau richtig – denn ohne dich und deine Idee wäre das re:publica-Programm nicht das, was es ist.

Vom 10.-12. Mai 2027 verwandeln wir die STATION Berlin in einen Ort für Austausch, Begegnungen, Debatten, Kunst und viele Überraschungen – und das bereits zum 20. Mal.

Sei dabei und gestalte die #rp27 mit!

Jetzt beim CfP einreichen

Warum du mitmachen solltest

Die re:publica lebt von euren Perspektiven. Von Menschen, die etwas zu sagen haben, die hinterfragen, um die Ecke denken, forschen, gestalten oder Debatten anstoßen. Von denen, die Projekte anschieben und umsetzen, Communities aufbauen oder Kunst schaffen, die berührt und zum Mitmachen einlädt. Wir freuen uns auf deine Expertise, deine Stimme, deine Kreativität – egal ob du zum ersten Mal dabei bist oder schon lange Teil der re:publica-Community.

Welche Formate du einreichen kannst

Für den Konferenzbereich kannst du folgende Formate einreichen:

- (Kurz-)Vortrag – Präsentationen zu einem Thema, allein oder zu zweit.
- Gespräch – Dialog oder Streitgespräch, mit oder ohne Moderation.
- Podiumsdiskussion – Moderiertes Gespräch mit verschiedenen Perspektiven.
- Podcast – Dein bestehender Podcast auf unserer Bühne.
- Meet Up – Offenes Treffen für Austausch mit der Community.
- Rede mit! – Interaktive oder dialogorientierte Formate wie Fishbowl.
- Workshop – Praktisch-partizipative Sessions zum Mitmachen.
- Nightlife – Kunst und Unterhaltung für die späteren Stunden!
- Embodiment – Körperbasierte Formate wie Bewegung oder Meditation.
- Sonderformat – Alles, was in keine Schublade passt.
Für den Off-Stage-Bereich kannst du folgende Formate einreichen:

- Installationen – Interaktive Arbeiten auf dem Festivalgelände.
- Spiele – Digitale oder analoge Games.
- Interventionen – Aktionen, die Raum und Publikum einbeziehen.
- DIY/Maker-Projekte – Mitmach-Formate und Projekte zum Ausprobieren.
- Sonderformate – Alles Ungewöhnliche und Überraschende.
Worauf es bei der Einreichung ankommt

Wichtig ist, dass dein Beitrag die Themen der digitalen Gesellschaft weiterdenkt: Von kritischen Fragen über neue Visionen bis zu konkreten Lösungen. Ob gesellschaftspolitisch, künstlerisch, technisch, wissenschaftlich, aktivistisch oder ganz persönlich – wir freuen uns auf deine Ideen, Perspektiven und Projekte!

Was uns besonders überzeugt:

- Relevanz, Aktualität & Lösungsorientierung
- Eigene Haltung und klare Perspektive
- Mehrwert für unser Publikum
- Vielfalt und Sichtbarkeit verschiedener Stimmen
Was uns nicht überzeugt:

- Marketing oder Sales-Pitch
- Buzzwords ohne Substanz
Das re:publica 27-Motto: #optinism

Opt-in heißt: bewusst Ja sagen, sich für etwas entscheiden. Optimismus heißt: daran glauben, dass Veränderung zum Positiven möglich ist. Zusammen wird daraus unser Motto für die re:publica 2027 .

Wir wollen mit euch diskutieren, experimentieren, streiten und neue Perspektiven entdecken. Denn nach 20 Jahren re:publica wissen wir: Eine bessere Zukunft fällt nicht vom Himmel. Sie braucht Menschen, die sich einmischen, Dinge hinterfragen und einfach mal anfangen.

Das Motto ist dabei unser gedanklicher Rahmen, keine thematische Schublade. Deine Einreichung muss sich nicht ausdrücklich auf das Motto beziehen.

Weitere Inspiration findest du in unseren diesjährigen Tracks und Schwerpunkt-Themen , oder du schaust dir die zahlreichen Videomitschnitte vergangener re:publica-Festivals auf unserem YouTube-Kanal an.

Alles, was du für deine Einreichung wissen musst, haben wir hier für dich zusammengestellt:

Hier geht's zum CfP

items.body:
# What Schools Still Don’t Teach About Interest Rates and Why It Matters | TeachThought

Most people leave school able to calculate interest on paper. Far fewer leave knowing what interest will do to their lives. That gap is easy to miss because it doesn’t show up on a report card. It shows up years later, in loan papers, credit card statements and savings balances that never seem to grow.

The problem isn’t that schools ignore math. Interest is taught as a formula, and the formula stops at the edge of the worksheet. Students learn how to find an answer but not how to read the numbers that will shape what they borrow, what they save and what they can afford. To close that gap, it helps to look at what gets left out, starting with how the subject is framed in the first place.

### The Gap Between Arithmetic and Everyday Money

### Formulas Without Consequences

A typical lesson on interest gives students a principal, a rate and a time period, then asks them to solve for the total. It’s tidy and it can be graded. It also hides almost everything that matters. Real rates change. Real balances get added to and drawn down. Real people make choices partway through, and those choices change the outcome.

When interest only ever appears as a problem with one right answer, students learn to treat it as a puzzle rather than as a force acting on their money every day.

### Interest Is a Price

The simplest idea missing from many classrooms is also the most useful one. Interest is the price of money over time. When you borrow, you pay that price. When you save, someone pays it to you. Once students see interest as a price, they start asking the questions they would ask about any purchase. Is this a good deal? Can I find it cheaper somewhere else? What happens if I wait?

That shift in thinking matters most when you see how interest builds over long stretches of time.

### How Compounding Actually Feels Over Time

### The Slow Start That Fools People

Compounding means you earn interest on your interest. Most students can repeat that definition. What they rarely get is a feel for how lopsided the results are.

Put $1,000 in an account earning 5% a year and leave it alone. In the first year, you earn $50. Nothing to get excited about. By year 30, the balance has grown to about $4,322, and that single year alone adds more than $200. The growth was always there, but it took decades to become obvious. People who expect fast results often give up during the slow early years, which is exactly when patience pays off most.

A quick shortcut called the rule of 72 makes this easier to grasp. Divide 72 by the interest rate, and you get a rough idea of how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, that’s about 12 years. A tool like the compound interest calculator on the SEC’s Investor.gov site lets students test different rates and time frames and watch the curve bend upward.

### Compounding Runs in Both Directions

The same math that rewards savers punishes borrowers. A credit card charging 24% APR works out to about 2% a month. On a $3,000 balance, that’s roughly $60 in interest in the first month. If you pay $75, only $15 actually goes toward what you owe. The balance barely moves, and the card company is happy to keep it that way.

Students who understand this early tend to treat credit cards very differently. Still, knowing how compounding works is only half the picture. The other half is knowing which rate you’re actually dealing with.

### Why the Rate You See Is Rarely the Rate You Pay

### APR, APY and the Fine Print

Banks and lenders use different terms for a reason. APR, or annual percentage rate, is often used for loans and doesn’t always show the effect of compounding. APY, or annual percentage yield, does. A 12% APR compounded monthly actually costs about 12.68% over a year. The gap looks small until it’s multiplied across a large balance or a long loan.

Few students are ever shown these two terms side by side. As a result, many adults compare offers without realizing they’re comparing different measurements.

### Inflation Eats Quietly

Even a correct rate can mislead you if inflation is ignored. If your savings earn 1% while prices rise 3%, your balance goes up but what it can buy goes down. Economists call the difference the real return. The Consumer Price Index published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics is the standard way to track how fast prices are rising, and checking it against your savings rate is a sobering exercise.

That raises a fair question. If rates matter this much, who decides what they are?

### Where Rates Come From

### The Central Bank’s Role

Rates don’t appear out of nowhere. In the United States, the Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate , which is what banks charge each other for overnight loans. That rate ripples outward into mortgages, car loans, credit cards and savings accounts.

### Why Your Rate Moves, or Doesn’t

Some rates follow the Fed closely. Variable credit card rates often rise within weeks of a hike. Others lag behind or barely move at all. Many large banks are slow to raise what they pay savers, even when borrowing costs climb. Knowing this helps people spot when they’re being underpaid and gives them a reason to act. The easiest place to put that knowledge to work is a savings account.

### Savings Accounts as a Practical Classroom

### Watching Interest Work in Real Time

A savings account turns abstract lessons into something you can see each month. Deposits go in, interest gets added and the balance changes without any effort. For a young person, watching even a few dollars of interest arrive can make compounding feel real in a way no textbook can. It also builds a habit, and habits tend to outlast lessons.

Savings accounts carry little risk, too. Deposits at insured banks are protected up to set limits, which makes them a calm place to learn how rates behave before moving on to investments that can lose value.

items.body:
The home page of Salon’s website in November 1999.

In the dying days of 1995, I was a freelance journalist in Portland, Oregon, who spent most of my time seated at a rickety particle-board desk, a gift from my father-in-law. The desk was covered in faux-walnut laminate and swayed from side to side as I wrote. I had already finished my main financial gusher for that year, a history book for fifth graders, and I needed more work.

In this respect I was no different than any freelancer in literary history. In fact, the technology involved in my trade, and the speed at which it functioned—its industrial metabolism—had hardly changed in the preceding century. Of course, I had a computer. But it hardly seemed to be much more than a glorified typewriter. And of course I had an email account, courtesy of the nerd Valhalla known as CompuServe. But the business of freelance journalism was still built largely around stuffing wads of paper into envelopes and sending them to editors, who would then transform the contents into other wads of paper: newspapers, magazines, books. The product, whatever you thought of it, was palpable.

Into this cozy Victorian setting came an online publication called Salon. It had been launched that same fall by a crew of ex-staffers from the San Francisco Examiner, traditional journalists trying to break the mold. I don’t remember which Salon editor contacted me in the first place. I do remember reading the website in my chilly little office, steadying the stupid desk with one leg and feeling an almost metaphysical puzzlement. Salon wasn’t some programmer’s hobby, whipped up in creaky old COBOL. It looked like a magazine, with zippy graphics and respectable fonts. The prose was smart, stylish, and amusingly contrarian.

All of this made a kind of sense to me. What was tricky was that it was free. That first afternoon, I printed out one of the articles, about The Beatles Anthology, which was just then airing on TV. I suppose I was turning back the technological clock—transubstantiating the product back into paper. Reading Salon gratis made me feel as if I were doing something furtive, as though I were a shoplifter, but it represented a kind of post-Gutenberg freedom.

Over the next year, I would write many pieces for Salon. I started out with book reviews that were assigned to me by Dwight Garner. (He had previously edited a few things of mine at Vogue, in terms of ethos the absolute inverse of Salon and, eventually, in terms of finances too.) Dwight sent me books by the bushel, or so it felt. I wrote very short pieces for him very quickly; they appeared online almost immediately. This, for the journalist, was unprecedented and nearly beggared belief. No more waiting for your piece to come out, pacing the equivalent of a widow’s walk. Sometimes I was even instructed to send the piece straight to the copy editor so we could cut a few more minutes out of the process.

Speediness of reflexes was part of the value proposition for Salon. Within months, the “smart tabloid,” as its founder David Talbot called it, was posting daily rather than weekly. In this way it inaugurated a fire-hose style of journalism that would in time become universal. The new norm was not waiting, not allowing stories to lose their heat in the cooling saucer of classic media.

Salon’s politics were similarly nontraditional: left-leaning, libertarian-adjacent (as per its Bay Area digs), but without an obvious party line. It doubtless helped that the magazine was not a subsidiary of a larger corporation, which was the case with Slate (part of Microsoft) and the earlier, cruder Mr. Showbiz (part of Starwave, a short-lived multimedia platform founded by Microsoft’s Paul Allen). Yes, Salon’s seed funding had come from Apple—a mingy $60,000—followed by a more substantial disbursement to the tune of $2 million from the Adobe cofounder John Warnock and various other investors. But it was an independent entity, unconstrained by the need to tiptoe around the feelings of a corporate proprietor.

In any case, I wasn’t writing about politics. I was writing about culture: the magazine’s strong suit. From books I branched into music—I believe it was Joyce Millman, Salon’s television critic, who assigned me pieces about Prince, Los Lobos, Bill Frisell, Cassandra Wilson. These were my enthusiasms, not the sort of dutiful, indiscriminate coverage that a film-critic friend of mine once likened to servicing a vending machine. I was allowed to venture further still when I pitched a piece about Martin Scorsese’s use of music. (The Casino soundtrack, I wrote, struck me as what the director might listen to “if he were shipwrecked with nothing but a polyester suit and a bank of slot machines.”)

It wasn’t long before I was writing short personal essays. I wrote one about being hoaxed by the founder of the Church of Kurt Cobain, which turned out to be nonexistent, although certainly plausible in the drizzling, grunge-friendly atmosphere of Portland. I wrote another about becoming addicted to All My Children during a serious family health crisis in the midst of which I found myself strangely inspired by the surreal resiliency of the characters, who never died unless their respective actor’s contracts with the show expired. I’m not making any extreme claims for these pieces. They were written at the madcap pace dictated by Salon and sandwiched between other freelance explorations—of dental malocclusion or aluminum smelting, say. For me, though, they still evoke the adrenaline feel of the period, the wild sense of participating in something new and transformative.

# Uganda Buddhist Centre campaign passes $1 million; new short film released

- Uganda Buddhist Centre campaign passes $1 million; new short film released | Lion’s Roar Uganda Buddhist Centre campaign passes $1 million; new short film released Supporters are halfway to the $2 million goal for protecting a Lake Victoria wetland and building Africa’s first dedicated retreat center, with $750,000 still needed by December 15. Rod Meade Sperry 25 November 2026 Bhante Buddharakkhita with His Holiness the Dalai Lama, who encouraged Bhante to pursue his vision for UBC. As seen in the new “Find Friends” video. Share Share Options
- Copy Link
- Facebook
- Email
The campaign to secure land for the Uganda Buddhist Centre (UBC) has passed $1 million, putting it halfway to its $2 million goal, organizers announced this week. Another $750,000 is needed to complete the land purchase by the December 15 deadline .

“What we do in the next three weeks decides whether this land is protected forever,” campaign organizer Leslie Booker wrote in the announcement.

### The story so far

Lion’s Roar first reported on the campaign in August, as UBC marked its 20th anniversary. Founded in 2005 by Bhante Buddharakkhita, UBC was the first Buddhist center in Uganda and the first in Africa established by an African monk. Its campus in Bulega-Garuga, near Entebbe, includes the Buddhist Peace School, the African Buddhist High School, and a medical center serving the surrounding community.

The campaign aims to buy 13 acres of wetland next to the campus, on the shores of Lake Nalubaale (Lake Victoria), the source of the Nile. Bhante Buddharakkhita plans to build what organizers describe as the first retreat center on the African continent dedicated solely to sharing the dhamma, and to protect the wetland permanently. If the land isn’t secured, it could be sold for a resort or a military base. Organizers warn that either would threaten food and water security for nearby schools, an orphanage, and surrounding villages.

In September, we reported that supporters had paid the $875,000 deposit needed to hold the land, and that the seller had extended the deadline for the remaining balance to December 15.

### “ Halfway home “

The $1.75 million asking price makes up most of the campaign’s $2 million goal. The rest covers surveys and unexpected costs. With $1 million raised, the $750,000 still needed by December 15 would complete the purchase itself.

Booker credited the campaign’s community for the milestone, saying every dollar came “from people like you,” through gifts large and small and through supporters sharing the campaign with others. Organizers are asking for “gratitude gifts” over the Thanksgiving week, whether it’s a donor’s first gift or their fifth. They’re also asking supporters to share the campaign with friends.

### A new film

The campaign has also released a short film, Find Friends: Bhante Buddharakkhita and the Uganda Buddhist Centre . It tells the story of UBC, Bhante Buddharakkhita’s vision for the land, and why protecting it matters. The film features Bhante Buddharakkhita and Booker.

“If you’ve ever tried to explain what Bhante means to you and couldn’t find the words, this film does it for you,” Booker wrote.

### How to help

Donations can be made through the campaign’s Chuffed page . Gifts are tax-deductible in the US. Donor-advised fund grants and employer matching gifts are also accepted. Supporters can also start a fundraising team with their sangha or friends through the same page.

Rod Meade Sperry

## The Map of Ancient Philosophy: Animation Shows How Socrates, Aristotle, Confucius, the Buddha & Other Great Thinkers Fit Together

in History , Maps , Philosophy | November 25th, 2026 Leave a Comment

-->

Here on Open Cul­ture, we’ve often fea­tured the charm­ing and infor­ma­tive posters of Domain of Sci­ence . Each one maps out a dif­fer­ent field of knowl­edge: there’s biol­o­gy , physics , chem­istry , quan­tum physics , quan­tum com­put­ing , fun­gi , and many oth­ers besides. But with his lat­est map, Domain of Sci­ence cre­ator Dominic Wal­li­man has turned away from the sci­en­tif­ic realm — or rather, he’s ven­tured into the larg­er intel­lec­tu­al ter­ri­to­ry out of which it emerged. His new Map of Phi­los­o­phy , which he explains in the video above , includes schools of thought going all the way back to 600 BC, and thinkers from antiq­ui­ty like Thales, Laozi, Con­fu­cius, and the Bud­dha, who lived and died before sci­ence as we know it.

That hard­ly means that they’ve become irrel­e­vant today. There still exist soci­eties described as Con­fu­cian or Bud­dhist, of course, but in the West­ern world, we’re more like­ly to refer back to — and, in many cas­es, have read a bit of — the work of Socrates, Pla­to, and Aris­to­tle. “They basi­cal­ly laid the intel­lec­tu­al foun­da­tion of West­ern phi­los­o­phy, sci­ence, and polit­i­cal thought,” says Wal­li­man. (He also reminds us that it was Socrates who said that the unex­am­ined life is not worth liv­ing, which “hits pret­ty hard in the age of the dis­trac­tion econ­o­my.”)

Though often men­tioned togeth­er, these three ancient Greeks occu­py slight­ly dif­fer­ent posi­tions on the philo­soph­i­cal map, with Socrates clos­er to the land of ethics, Pla­to to meta­physics, and Aris­to­tle to epis­te­mol­o­gy.

As Wal­li­man explains, “epis­te­mol­o­gy stud­ies knowl­edge: what it is, where it comes from, and also how it dif­fers from faith or opin­ions,” while also seek­ing out its lim­its. Aris­totle’s rig­or in test­ing and orga­niz­ing knowl­edge makes him, in a sense, one of the ear­li­est sci­en­tists. Though his body of the­o­ry may no longer be our best means of under­stand­ing how the world works, his sys­tem­at­ic pur­suit of such an under­stand­ing set him apart from much of the ancient intel­lec­tu­al world. The islands off the coast of the map’s main­land rep­re­sent sub­fields still active­ly explored today, like the philoso­phies of mind, lan­guage, pol­i­tics, reli­gion, and sci­ence — which, for all its pres­tige, remains as sub­ject to philo­soph­i­cal inquiry as any oth­er area of human endeav­or. The map of phi­los­o­phy shows us not a rar­efied, most­ly aban­doned ter­ri­to­ry, but the place where we all live our lives, exam­ined or oth­er­wise.

Pla­to, Aris­to­tle & Oth­er Greek Philoso­phers in Raphael’s Renais­sance Mas­ter­piece, The School of Athens

items.body:
## the moving architecture of the concept car

When Pininfarina presented its **[Ferrari](https://www.designboom.com/tag/ferrari/) 512S Modulo** at the 1970 Geneva Motor Show, the Italian design team brought a vision of the [automobile](https://www.designboom.com/tag/car-design/) with almost all its familiar elements erased. The wheels were partially hidden beneath a white body, the roof barely rose above the hood, and the continuous black band of glazing gave little indication of how someone might get inside. To enter Paolo Martin’s futuristic [concept car](https://www.designboom.com/tag/car-concept/), the entire canopy had to slide forward.

The Modulo belongs to a radical period in automotive design when coachbuilders began to rethink the simple act of entering a car. With the freedom afforded by experimental prototypes, designers could do away with typical doors and set in motion much larger portions of the body. A windshield could become an entrance, and a roof could lift away to expose the entire cabin.

Read on as we revisit a series of these experiments from the 1960s through the end of the century. While much of the discussion around automotive design concerns the appearance of speed, these cars reveal some of their most dynamic qualities while standing perfectly still.

1970 Ferrari 512S Modulo concept

1970 Ferrari 512S Modulo concept

## car designers made the door disappear

Seven years before the Modulo made its debut, a young Giorgetto Giugiaro had explored the possibilities of a continuous automotive shell with the **[Chevrolet](https://www.designboom.com/tag/chevrolet/) Corvair Testudo**. Designed at Bertone and presented in Geneva in 1963, the car had a distinctly organic profile. Its name, the Latin word for tortoise, alluded to the rounded body beneath which much of the mechanical equipment was concealed. The glass windshield and roof formed part of a single assembly that pivoted forward to expose the two seats.

The Testudo emerged at a time when the futuristic imagery of aviation and space exploration had entered the vocabulary of industrial design. The aircraft canopy offered an alternative to the upright door inherited from the horse-drawn carriage, and its application to the automobile gave designers greater freedom over the shape of the passenger compartment. The legendary designer could draw an uninterrupted line along the flank of his car because the point of entry had been moved elsewhere.

Paolo Martin took Giugiaro’s idea to an extreme with the **Ferrari Modulo** in 1970. Built on the chassis of a Ferrari 512S racing car, the concept was composed of two broad, almost horizontal volumes separated by a fine red line. The glazed upper enclosure sat within this geometry like the retractable roof of a building. In photographs of the Modulo with its canopy open, the familiar proportions of the car give way to an unexpected arrangement of overlapping planes.

1963 Chevrolet Corvair Testudo | image courtesy Carrozzeria Bertone

1963 Chevrolet Corvair Testudo | image courtesy Carrozzeria Bertone

## marcello gandini and the theater of arrival

At Bertone, Marcello Gandini approached the question of entry from an entirely different direction. His copper-colored **Lancia Stratos Zero**, unveiled at the 1970 Turin Motor Show, stood just 84 centimeters (33 inches) tall. Its sharply angled profile was partly the product of an exercise within the design studio to see how low a car could possibly be built.

There is a small black rectangle at the base of the Stratos Zero’s windshield, which could easily be mistaken for a decorative detail. It is actually a rubber mat designed to accommodate the feet of someone stepping onto the bodywork. Beneath the Lancia badge is a concealed handle that releases the hinged windshield, while a hydraulic linkage connects the movement of the glass to that of the steering column.

Where most cars are approached from the side, the Stratos Zero asks its occupants to walk directly toward its nose, step onto its sloping surface, and lower themselves into the reclining seats. Gandini effectively designed a sequence of arrival around the geometry of the wedge. The exterior bodywork takes on some of the functions of a building’s entrance, right down to its little doorstep.

1970 Lancia Stratos HF Zero | image courtesy [Petersen Automotive Museum](https://petersen.org/pages/petersen-vehicle/1970-lancia-stratos-hf-zero)

1970 Lancia Stratos HF Zero | image courtesy Petersen Automotive Museum

## when the car moved to receive the human body

While Italian coachbuilders experimented with increasingly extreme proportions, designers at General Motors were developing cars whose interiors could physically accommodate the movements of their occupants.

At the 1967 New York Auto Show, Chevrolet introduced its **Astro I**, an aerodynamic research vehicle designed by Larry Shinoda under the direction of Bill Mitchell. The red fiberglass body stood only 90 centimeters (35.5 inches) high, and a large section of its upper body hinged upward from the rear. Inside, the seats rose with the canopy.

1967 Chevrolet Astro I | image © GM

1967 Chevrolet Astro I | image © GM

## a dynamic and responsive interior

Two years later, on the other side of the world, General Motors’ Australian division introduced the metallic orange **Holden Hurricane**. Its hydraulically operated canopy pivoted forward over the front wheels, while the two seats rose and tilted toward the opening. The steering column moved out of the way. Once the occupants had climbed aboard, the seats descended into a reclining driving position and the roof closed above them.

items.body:
# Shamash Alidina: Gratitude with Room for Everything Else

Gratitude practices sometimes feel like one more thing to get right, as if we’re supposed to feel thankful on cue no matter what’s happening.

Our guest this week is Shamash Alidina. He offers a gentler approach. You make room for whatever you’re feeling, and then you see whether one small, ordinary thing you appreciate can sit alongside it.

In this meditation, you’ll:

- Acknowledge how life is for you right now
- Hold difficulty and appreciation side by side
- Connect gratitude to what you value, rather than just how you feel
## Shamash Alidina: Gratitude with Room for Everything Else

Read and practice this meditation on your own, pausing after each step. Or listen to the guided audio.

- Find a comfortable position and let your body settle. You can close your eyes or keep them open with a soft, relaxed gaze. There’s nothing to achieve here. You don’t need to feel calm, happy, or grateful. You’re simply giving yourself a little time to be here.
- Notice the places where your body makes contact with what’s beneath you. Feel the gentle movement of your breath. There’s no need to change it. Just notice the body breathing in and breathing out.
- Allow whatever you’re experiencing to be here. Maybe your mind is busy or your body feels restless. That’s fine. There’s nothing you need to fix.
- Bring to mind how life is for you at the moment. Perhaps something is worrying you. Maybe you’re missing someone, feeling lonely, or facing a challenge. Or perhaps things are going reasonably well. Whatever you notice, acknowledge it honestly. You might silently say, This is what I’m experiencing right now.
- Notice any feeling in your body that comes with this experience. It might be tightness, heaviness, or restlessness. You don’t need to make it go away. Imagine making room for it the way you’d make room for a visitor at your door. You don’t have to invite it to stay forever. Just acknowledge that it’s here. For these few moments, there’s no need to talk yourself out of how you feel. Let yourself be a human being with human experiences.
- With the difficulty in the background, look for one small thing you appreciate. It might be someone who cares about you, a place where you feel safe, a warm drink, a comfortable bed, or a memory of laughter. Something quite ordinary is enough. If nothing comes to mind, that’s perfectly fine. Simply notice the support beneath your body or feel your feet on the floor. You don’t have to produce gratitude on demand.
- If you’ve found something, take a little time with it. What about this person, place, or experience matters to you? Maybe it brings warmth, comfort, connection, or relief. Maybe it’s simply pleasant. Don’t force the feeling to be bigger than it is.
- Notice the details. If it’s a memory, recall it gently. If it’s happening now, explore it through your senses. Let yourself receive the experience rather than hurrying on to the next thing.
- Hold both the difficult and the good. You don’t need to get rid of a difficult feeling to appreciate something good. You can feel worried and still enjoy being supported. You can feel sad and remember someone you love. You can feel lonely and appreciate a small, kind interaction. Imagine holding the difficulty in one hand and this small appreciation in the other.
- Consider what this moment of appreciation points toward. Is there something you value in it, such as connection, kindness, friendship, health, creativity, or a little space to stop and breathe? Is there one small action you could take today to bring more of it into your life? You could send someone a message, step outside, take a proper break, or offer yourself a little more patience. If today is hard, the kindest thing may be to allow yourself some rest or support. Gratitude doesn’t require you to pretend everything is fine.
- Return to your surroundings. Notice your breathing, the sounds around you, and the support beneath your body. When you’re ready, gently open your eyes if they’ve been closed, and bring some gentle movement into your body.
- Thank yourself for taking these few minutes. May you find room for both the difficult moments and the small moments of goodness in the days ahead.
### About The Author

### Shamash Alidina

Shamash Alidina has been practising mindfulness since 1998 and runs his own successful training organisation. He is the author of Mindfulness For Dummies and most recently, The Mindful Way Through Stress . He frequently pops up in newspapers, magazines and on radio shows. Based in London, he runs online trainings and speaks at conferences all over the world. He’s been teaching mindfulness full-time since 2010.

items.body: Background: Individuals with limited English proficiency (LEP) or limited host-language proficiency (LLP) represent a growing, medically underserved population at disproportionate risk for poor mental health outcomes. Most mental and behavioral health services provided to individuals with LEP or LLP are delivered by providers who do not speak the patient’s preferred language, due to a shortage of bilingual mental health professionals. Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of telehealth-delivered outpatient mental health (telemental) visits has increased, yet little is understood about the provision of interpretation and/or translation-facilitated telemental health care in populations with LEP and LLP. Objective: This study is a scoping review that aimed to characterize the existing evidence on interpretation- and translation-mediated telemental health services for adults with LEP or LLP. We examined study characteristics, populations, and settings represented, telemental health modalities used, reported barriers and facilitators, and the methodological quality and gaps within the current evidence base. Methods: Included studies focused on adults receiving interpreter and/or translation-mediated telemental health services. All studies were published in the English language, which may limit generalizability. Studies with bilingual providers, nonbehavioral health care, mobile health (mHealth) applications, or deaf or hard-of-hearing populations were excluded. Online databases were used to identify papers published through May 2026, from which we selected 15 publications from 137 full-text articles retrieved for full-text screening. Results: A total of 60% (9/15) of publications reported qualitative or mixed method designs, while 40% (6/15) were quantitative. Most were conducted with Spanish-speaking populations. Of the 15 studies, 12 achieved >4 out of 5 using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Thematic analysis yielded the following four themes across the articles reviewed: (1) facilitators of access, (2) barriers to access, (3) therapeutic process considerations, and (4) recommendations to improve quality of and access to interpreter- or translation-mediated telemental health care in LEP and LLP populations. Conclusions: As previous reviews focused primarily on in-person mental health care, this scoping review is among the first to synthesize evidence specifically on interpreter and translation-mediated telemental health for individuals with LEP or LLP. In addition, its inclusion of literature published after COVID-19 allowed for an examination of how the literature has evolved from the prepandemic period to the post-2020 telemental health expansion. Findings underscored the following needs: (1) address access barriers to telemental health care in populations with LEP and LLP, which persist following the postpandemic increase in telemental health adoption; (2) standardize training for clinicians and interpreters; and (3) update clinical guidelines in the context of rapid telehealth uptake in behavioral health care. It also highlighted the potential impact of emerging AI technologies for real-time translation in mental health care, calling for further research on their ethical and clinical implications.

## Marina Herlop ~ Dja Dja

Marina Herlop ‘s Dja Dja unfolds like a picaresque adventure through an enchanted world, populated by witches, angels, wolves and other less identifiable creatures. There are moments of childlike wonder, encounters with darker forces and sudden changes of scenery. The Catalan composer’s fifth album, following Pripyat (2022) and Nekkuja (2023), is also her most ambitious undertaking: fifteen interconnected pieces loosely following the archetypal hero’s journey. From the outset, it reveals itself as a beguiling treasure trove of an album.

Herlop has described the process of composing Dja Dja as something akin to solving a giant sudoku. In an interview with The Creative Independent , she explained that she wanted to approach the album as a novel rather than a collection of short stories, mapping out its harmonic, rhythmic and instrumental relationships in advance. This intricate planning is reflected in the recurring melodies and vocal phrases that connect seemingly disparate compositions. “Vas volant” and “Siete mares” share the same invented syllables, while the melody of the former resurfaces in “Lilit”. The words of “As meigas”, meanwhile, return in “Bliss”, with their disturbing references to murderous angels.

Although rooted in Herlop’s Catalan background, the album’s linguistic world extends well beyond it. Catalan, Spanish, Galician and other languages appear in the titles, while recognisable lyrics coexist with her characteristic invented vocabulary. In a 2024 interview with Goûte Mes Disques , Herlop spoke of her growing desire to sing in Catalan, concerned that the increasing dominance of English might eventually erase certain expressions from her native language. Yet language in her music is rarely confined to communication. Words and syllables are chosen as much for their phonetic qualities as for their meaning, allowing the voice to become an instrument in its own right.

The opening “Flor de los precipicios” introduces this peculiar world through Herlop’s acrobatic singing and a prominent flute, one of several wind instruments that provide much of the musical scaffolding of the album’s early stages. With “Vas volant”, the adventure gathers momentum, the music taking flight through a succession of buoyant electronic figures and intricately arranged vocal patterns. “ツラ” conjures something resembling an imaginary bioacoustic environment, alive with unfamiliar calls and rustling activity. Elsewhere, the metallic percussion of Balinese gamelan enters Herlop’s increasingly elaborate musical constructions.

As the journey progresses, keyboards and brass acquire greater prominence. “Jaque” introduces a more confrontational atmosphere, its forceful instrumental gestures suggesting a contest of musical wills, while the exuberant “Los dos lobos” pits looping voices against unruly percussion and swaggering brass. The effect is often wonderfully absurd, as though the inhabitants of an elaborate cabinet of curiosities had suddenly sprung to life and begun arguing among themselves.

But the journey also has its moments of defeat. “You’ve Lost Your Muchness”, a title borrowed from the world of Alice in Wonderland , is a brief, disorientating interlude populated by strange, gurgling voices and fleeting electronic apparitions. Herlop has identified it as the album’s lowest point, deliberately removing the comforting familiarity of repetition to create an atmosphere of unease. The gently articulated guitar of “Hay ángeles” then brings the music back to more recognisably human territory, before “Average Evil” stages another lively encounter between competing rhythmic figures and sharply articulated vocal syllables.

“Bliss” erupts into a joyous collision of bass, percussion and vocal acrobatics, culminating in a flurry of synths. But the album refuses to end on such a victorious note. Instead, “Muy heladas” returns to the frozen landscape evoked near the beginning, gradually expanding into solemn, almost liturgical orchestral harmonies. The journey has come full circle, although its destination remains ambiguous.

For all the painstaking calculations behind its construction, Dja Dja retains a sense of mischief and unpredictability. Herlop has spoken of feeling that the music was pulling her away from her carefully laid plans, and there is something of that struggle in the finished work. Its strange inhabitants seem to have acquired a life of their own, occasionally escaping the elaborate architecture designed to contain them. Perhaps that is where the album’s peculiar magic lies.

Photo by Silvio Deiaco, Danilo Gambara, Christian Kondić

To expand on the musical journey, we reached out to Marina Herlop.

You’ve described the making of Dja Dja as something akin to solving a giant sudoku, with an elaborate system of harmonic, rhythmic and instrumental relationships mapped out in advance. Yet, listening to the album, I was struck by how unpredictable and mischievous it feels, almost as though its strange inhabitants had acquired lives of their own. You’ve also spoken about the music sometimes pulling you away from your original plans. How did you negotiate that tension between imposing a rigorous structure and allowing the music to take unexpected turns? Were there moments when you had to abandon your carefully laid plans altogether?

items.body:
[Adobe](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/adobe/) has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing users with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives "more time for their craft".

Unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference in Miami Beach on 10 November, the update spans the brand’s flagship Creative Cloud tools.

The updates were unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference

[Photoshop](https://www.adobe.com/products/photoshop.html) now features generative restyle and relight, [Premiere](https://www.adobe.com/products/premiere.html) has a new colour mode, and [InDesign](https://www.adobe.com/products/indesign.html) now supports co-editing (beta).

Adobe is also bringing the Creative Agent to [Firefly](https://news.adobe.com/news/2026/11/adobe-firefly-expands) – its AI creative studio – through the [Firefly AI Assistant, which is currently in beta](https://www.adobe.com/products/firefly/features/ai-assistant.html).

Users can direct the assistant in plain language, with Adobe stating it has already been used for everything from batch retouching portraits to turning product shots into short-form social videos.

The aim is to help creators take on projects that may previously have required more time, resources or technical complexity.

Adobe has also launched [Firefly Design](https://www.adobe.com/products/firefly/features/design.html) in beta, a single workspace that combines raster and vector graphics with motion, 3D and print design.

Available as part of Creative Cloud, Firefly Design allows designers to build, review, and hand over projects without leaving the platform.

The conference took place at Miami Beach on 10 November

Topaz Labs, now part of Adobe, has released two new image-enhancement models, Wonder 4 and Image HDR, which are sold separately through Topaz.

Adobe said the Creative Cloud updates respond to the way creatives are increasingly working – juggling more formats, apps and mediums while being asked to turn projects around faster.

The brand's latest approach aims to tackle this by bringing "AI assistance and collaboration directly into the Adobe tools they rely on".

Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud at Adobe, said the aim is to protect what makes a creative’s work distinctive.

“The ideas, taste, style and vision that creative professionals bring to their work are what make their work stand out,” said Subramaniam.

“Our latest Creative Cloud innovations transform our trusted creative tools into agentic, intelligent workflows that give pros the precision, control and flexibility to explore their ideas, streamline their work and stay focused on the creative decisions that make their work uniquely theirs.”

The updates aim to help creators take on more complex projects

The Creative Agent – which Adobe describes as a creative partner – now powers AI Assistants (currently in beta) across Premiere, [Illustrator](https://www.adobe.com/products/illustrator.html), InDesign, [After Effects](https://www.adobe.com/products/aftereffects.html) and [Frame.io](https://frame.io/). In Photoshop, the assistant is available only in the Photoshop beta app.

The agent handles multi-step tasks behind the scenes, letting professionals delegate work and increase their creative velocity while remaining "in the director’s chair".

In Premiere, the agent now supports new capabilities, including applying an effect to every clip in a sequence, tracking a masked subject through a frame, and adjusting colour and exposure across a whole sequence at once.

Adobe is also previewing local MCP integrations, which allow external AI agents to connect with its software.

Adobe is also bringing the Creative Agent to Firefly

The integrations will let users instruct third-party agents of their choice to work inside Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects, editing project files directly on their own computer.

Layers, vectors and sequences stay fully editable throughout the process, so users can "step in at any moment to refine the work by hand". The local MCP integrations will be available in private beta in early 2027.

If a user’s chosen third-party agent is also connected to other MCP-capable tools, such as Google Drive or Slack, it can bring them into the same workflow. For example, it could pull in a brief from Google Docs, work on the project using Adobe’s tools and share the result with colleagues in Slack.

Adobe has also added several updates that give Firefly users more say over how the AI assistant works. Creatives are now able to save their preferred formats, colours, brand guidelines, characters and products to be applied consistently in future projects.

A new plan mode lets users review, edit and approve the agent’s plan before it starts, or leave the agent to run on its own. Adobe explained that creators remain in control, "guiding the work and making creative decisions as their projects evolve".

Users can also choose which AI model the agent works with, or let the agent select the best fit for the task.

The workflows will give creatives "more time for their craft"

In [Firefly Boards](https://www.adobe.com/products/firefly/features/boards.html), the agent can help develop mood boards, storyboards and concepts through conversation as they take shape in real time, “guided by human taste and direction".

Adobe also introduced a preview of always-on agents to carry out routine jobs, such as sorting new files or preparing content for different platforms, “even when the customer steps away".

Firefly’s video, design and image editors have also been updated, with the aim of taking projects from initial idea to finished work in a single workflow.

items.body: Advances in brain-machine interfaces and neuroprosthetics are often framed as a path toward overcoming the biological limits of the body, with the eventual replacement of failing limbs and organs by durable artificial substitutes. Interestingly, this optimistic narrative overlooks a challenge that is becoming increasingly apparent in aging neuroscience: brain health depends critically on a continuous supply of trophic signals originating from skeletal muscle and bone. Myokines and osteokines such as irisin, uncarboxylated osteocalcin, and cathepsin B act on the brain to sustain BDNF expression, synaptic plasticity, and neurogenesis, forming what has been described as a muscle-bone-brain axis; disuse and immobilization, even in the absence of any primary brain pathology, are sufficient to disrupt this signaling and accelerate cognitive decline. This raises a largely unaddressed question for cyborg technologies: could a robotic body, mechanically capable of movement but biologically inert and secreting none of the trophic factors that living muscle and bone normally provide, deprive the brain of signals it needs to remain healthy, thereby accelerating, rather than preventing, neural aging? We term this hypothetical condition cyborg dementia. Rather than a purely engineering problem of motor control and sensory feedback, this reframes brain-machine interface design as fundamentally about preserving the endocrine dialogue between brain and musculoskeletal system, extending the goals of neuroprosthetics beyond restoring action to protecting the neuroendocrine mechanisms that biological embodiment was silently providing all along.

items.body:
Donald Trump after returning to the White House from Walter Reed National Military Medical Center on Oct. 5, 2020. Win McNamee/Getty Images.

Happy Thanksgiving Eve! I think we have a good little newsletter for you today, but let me link to this week’s Still Counting episode first:

Video above, audio below. In case you’re [stuck on the tarmac somewhere](https://www.natesilver.net/p/how-soon-should-you-arrive-at-the-airport), we tried to have some fun, talking about the [Trump-backed restoration of Jensen Huang at Nvidia](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cq5y1k8ez407o), the [Democrats’ debate schedule](https://democrats.org/dnc-announces-framework-for-the-2028-democratic-presidential-primary-debates/), and answering several listener questions. And yes, our Thanksgiving wish is that you’ll comment, [like](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/still-counting/id6804845033), review and/or subscribe to the show.

#### The context

President Trump’s approval rating has [steadily declined over the past two years.](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin) Believe me: we get some things wrong around these parts. We have before and we will again. But the idea that [second terms hit different and have much lower approval floors](https://www.natesilver.net/p/how-low-is-trumps-popularity-floor) was one of those points on which we were a little ahead of the curve.

Subscribe now

On the podcast, we talked about how poorly Trump has performed as some kind of “populist”. I’m sorry if any of this comes across as partisan, but I’m trying to describe reality. In various ways, he’s betrayed his base.

The “Liberation Day” tariffs triggered an initial decline in Trump’s numbers, but at least they were [broadly consistent](https://www.c-span.org/clip/campaign-2024/donald-trump-on-trade-and-tariffs/5121548) with what he’d promised on the campaign trail. Going to war with Iran and spiking gas prices as a result [wasn’t](https://www.natesilver.net/p/will-iran-break-maga) what he advertised, however. I[don’t want to overindex on this](https://www.natesilver.net/p/is-epstein-the-new-russiagate), but talking a big game about releasing the Epstein files and then basically reneging wasn’t consistent with his promises either.

And then there’s [this Nvidia story](https://www.natesilver.net/p/the-nvidia-story-is-a-bfd) — and the broader embrace of Silicon Valley by the president and [vice versa](https://www.natesilver.net/p/silicon-valleys-gamble-on-trump-isnt). Look, I respect Jensen Huang, and I don’t care who he slept with. Silicon Valley types almost seem to be promoting angles about his reported infidelity or his [reported abusive treatment of staffers](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/jensen-huang-back-nvidia-staff-223000688.html) because it obscures the real issue here: that Nvidia’s best chips were [reportedly winding up in the hands of China](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/u-s-works-to-close-loophole-that-let-china-access-advanced-ai-chips).

AI is the [most important technology of my lifetime](https://www.natesilver.net/p/ai-is-moving-way-too-fast), and one of the most important in the history of the human species. It also plausibly follows winner-take-all dynamics, and it obviously has [national security implications](https://www.natesilver.net/p/anthtropic-open-ai-department-of-war). I don’t think Huang’s position is incoherent. Maybe American leadership in the sector is so strong that we can afford to export Blackwell chips to China because we’re not going to forsake the lead. And [maybe AI is a “normal technology](https://knightcolumbia.org/content/ai-as-normal-technology),” as I think Huang and Nvidia honestly believe — although I don’t think they have much remaining credibility on the matter.

But Trump[ran as a “China hawk.](https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/05/12/trump-china-hawk-xi-jinping-covid/)” Because I basically do think that [AI is an](https://www.natesilver.net/p/the-singularity-wont-be-gentle) *[extraordinary](https://www.natesilver.net/p/the-singularity-wont-be-gentle)* [technology](https://www.natesilver.net/p/the-singularity-wont-be-gentle), and I’d put nuclear weapons in the same category, I’m going to make the obvious comparison here. What if Ronald Reagan had run as a USSR/Russia hawk, and yet also helped to facilitate the export of fissile material toward the Russians? I think he’d have been impeached and removed from office.

In making political forecasts, you’re often stuck between a rock and a hard place. Clearly we’re living in times of extremely high partisanship, and clearly also Trump retains a lot of influence on Republican legislators and executives. That caps his downside to some extent. But his ability to intimidate is severely negated after a completely *embarrassing* midterm result for the GOP. His party just lost a Senate seat in Missis-fucking-sippi. He’s never cared about anyone other than himself, and to the extent he worries about his popularity over the next two years at all, he [seems to be unable to behave rationally](https://www.natesilver.net/p/the-white-house-needs-a-ground-stop). He’s 80 years old. I’m not even going to speculate about how and whether Trump Inc. is profiting off of chip sales to China, though there’s obviously room for responsible inferences on that question. (He [does own a fair bit of Nvidia stock](https://www.reuters.com/technology/nvidia-reinstates-jensen-huang-ceo-2026-11-23/).)

…

items.body:
The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks.

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the [Vancouver Art Gallery](https://www.vanartgallery.bc.ca/art-of-wellbeing/), and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend [PaRx](https://www.parkprescriptions.ca/), Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access.

Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.

*Credit: Vancouver Art Gallery*

## An artful approach to treatment

The process starts when a health care provider like a doctor, nurse, or therapist determines that a patient might benefit from a prescription to spend time in nature, including around the nature-inspired visual art at the gallery. The benefits can be many: combating isolation, engaging mentally and physically during a gallery visit, and experiencing awe and beauty.

The prescription to Vancouver Art Gallery includes free admission for the prescription holder and a guest, as well as a printed guide that offers prompts and questions to consider—for example, to notice the varied shades of green Carr used, or imagine a walk along a trail she painted—along with research about the benefits of experiencing nature. Participants are guided through “slow looking” as the act of learning through observation, imagination exercises, and physical movement—yes, swaying in an art gallery is encouraged.

After the visit, guests are invited to continue the immersion at a local nature space, with free carshare minutes to get there if needed. The art prescription guide suggests nearby parks where participants can walk or hike, extending slow looking from a curated indoor experience to the outdoors if they choose. And they can return to the gallery as often as they like by retaining their original prescription. On site, they can join free workshops, and a coloring book offers a contemplative experience at home.

This is an example of social prescribing, a worldwide movement that serves as a complement to clinical care and typical medication prescriptions by prescribing from a wide range of activities that support physical and mental health. Beyond art galleries and nature walks, this can include music classes, exercise sessions, or gardening programs. The prescription is personal and can be tailored to patients’ needs and interests.

Carla Fry is a West Vancouver psychologist and educator with more than 20 years of clinical experience. She says the art gallery prescription has been a gift for participants, especially those who face physical, mental, social, or even financial or transportation barriers to accessing nature. Many are surprised that they don’t have to pay anything for the experience.

“For them to understand that so many people have come together to create this opportunity, I think that in and of itself is special,” Fry says. “They say, ‘Wow, my community cares.’ The possibility that this exists, it’s available, it’s free—there’s something about that... that’s noteworthy.”

Fry is one of the professionals who gives these kinds of prescriptions to her clients. It’s another tool available to promote well-being.

“Of course, I’m never telling them to go. We talk about this as a prescription, but I always present it as ‘here’s an opportunity to meet some of your goals, and here’s what the opportunity looks like,’” she says.

As yet, no one has declined her prescription.

“They’re surprised that something so seemingly simplistic as slowing down and really looking, really living in front of the art or in nature is actually an intervention,” Fry says. “People in our culture are set up to think that growth has got to be painful, growth has got to be difficult, growth has got to be expensive, growth is going to take a long time. When I bring forward an intervention of going to a location, and your job as a client of mine is to appreciate, the first reaction is surprise. It opens up an entire conversation—‘I can just appreciate my life and not always be grinding to make it better.’ It’s a special process for me to witness.”

## Awe and nature in community

The goal is to do more than increase the number of people who have exposure to art, though that might be a side effect. The formal prescription to nature through art is designed to reduce stress, anxiety, and social isolation. The ability to bring a guest, as well as the opportunity to experience art with other patrons, is key.

items.body:
# Erica Synths EDU DIY Reverb Kit Uses Two BBD Chips To Build An Analog Room Simulator

Erica Synths and Moritz Klein have introduced the EDU DIY Reverb , an educational kit that guides builders through designing a fully analog reverb Eurorack module, using two bucket-brigade delay (BBD) chips.

The project starts with a breadboard prototype that simulates a room, then develops into a 10HP Eurorack module.

The circuit uses the two BBD chips to create a simulated room without springs, plates or digital processing. The accompanying illustrated manual explains the circuit design and takes builders through the process of developing the effect, from the breadboard stage to the finished module.

The completed module provides controls for tone, decay and room size, with voltage control over decay and room size. Erica Synths says the effect can produce anything from short ambience to self-oscillation. The module shares its 10HP footprint with the EDU DIY BBD, allowing owners of the KONSTRUKT-8 system to swap the BBD module for the Reverb.

Features:

- Educational DIY project developed by Erica Synths and Moritz Klein
- Fully analog, solid-state reverb based on two BBD chips
- Breadboard-based circuit design and experimentation before module assembly
- Illustrated manual explaining the circuit and build process
- Controls for tone, decay and room size
- Voltage control over decay and room size
- Sound range from short ambience to self-oscillation
- 10HP Eurorack module
- Same footprint as the EDU DIY BBD module, for compatibility with the KONSTRUKT-8 system
Pricing & Availability:

The Erica Synths EDU DIY Reverb DIY kit is priced at €85, excluding VAT, and is available directly from the manufacturer.

items.body:
Built in 1840, this one-room School House served as the educational center for all of the first to eighth grade children in the Hockanum area, later serving only up to sixth grade. This was one of several school houses serving small neighborhood communities around Hadley.

A 1647 Massachusetts law required all towns with 50 or more families to hire a teacher to instruct their children in reading and writing. Parents and students contributed to their school in the form of money, goods, supplies, and chores.

These were one-room schoolhouses, on land that was usually donated. Most schools had one book, the "New England Primer," that was used to teach the alphabet, syllables, and prayer.

The last class to go through this school was in 1933. By then, it was more economical to bus students to the center of town than to keep the neighborhood school houses open.

Along with the outhouse next to it, the Hockanum School House was, and still is, taken care of by the Hockanum community.
